warmup.q: A follower keeps up by running the leader's instructions again, in the same order, a moment later. Which instruction is certain to leave the follower's data the same as the leader's?
options: Add a refund of 5.00 for payment 41, stamped with the current time
Add 5.00 to account 7's balance, when a follower that reconnects may be sent it twice
Delete any 1,000 saved receipts whose expiry time has passed by now
warmup.why: Setting a fixed value on one record, found by its number, gives the same result on any machine, even if it runs twice. "The current time" is read from the follower's own clock, which is later than the leader's. An instruction that adds to a balance adds twice if it arrives twice. "Any 1,000" lets each machine delete whichever 1,000 it meets first, which can differ, and "by now" reads the clock again. Logs that carry the resulting values avoid all three, as the third section shows.

sections.h: Sending the statement: short, readable, and different on every machine
sections.html:
Here's a change the leader might make at the end of a day, when the company pays each shop what it took: UPDATE payments SET status = 'paid_out' WHERE batch_id = 42. That line is SQL, the language most databases take commands in, and one command is called a statement. This one marks every payment in batch 42 as paid out to its shop. What should the leader's log say about it? Real databases give three answers, and each fails in its own way.

The simplest answer is the statement itself. The leader writes those 59 bytes to the log, and every follower runs the same statement. One entry can change 80,000 rows. A person can read the log. And a follower running another version of the database understands it, as long as the SQL means the same thing there. MySQL, a popular free database, copied changes only this way until version 5.1.

It breaks because a statement is a small program, and each follower runs it somewhere else, later. Anything that depends on where or when it runs can come out different:

  • now() and random(), which return the current time and a random number. The follower works them out with its own clock and its own random numbers. In this section's demo, the follower runs each statement 350 ms after the leader, so every time it records is 350 ms later. And each payment's reference code, made from a random number, differs.
  • New ids, when two clients write at once. Each new row takes the next number from a counter, an auto-increment id. Two clients add a row each (an insert) at the same moment. The first takes id 7, the second id 8, but the second commits, becomes final, first. The log is in commit order, so the follower runs the second insert first and gives it id 7.
  • Statements whose result depends on row order. DELETE FROM payments WHERE merchant = 'm2' LIMIT 100 deletes whichever 100 of that shop's payments the database meets first (the lab calls a shop a merchant). A follower that was loaded from a copy stores its rows in another order, so it deletes other rows.
  • Changes that add to a value, arriving twice. SET fee = fee + 30 is right once. If a follower that reconnects is sent the entry again, as in lesson 1's catch-up, it charges the fee again.
  • Triggers, small programs the database runs on every change to a table, and functions with side effects. A trigger that stamps now() on every change, or a function that calls another program, runs again on every follower.

The leader can repair some of this by writing values into the log. MySQL records the leader's clock time with each statement, so its manual treats NOW() as safe. It flags statements that use RAND(), UUID(), SYSDATE() or USER(), and updates with LIMIT, as unsafe. Its log has three formats, STATEMENT, ROW and MIXED. In STATEMENT, an unsafe statement only earns a warning; in MIXED, it's logged as rows instead (the third section). MySQL 8.0 also made a faster way of handing out new ids the default, one that's unsafe for statement logs, because by then MySQL logged rows by default.

The PostgreSQL manual warns about programs that send the same SQL to several servers, such as Pgpool-II, which sits between clients and a group of PostgreSQL servers. In its words, random(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and sequences (PostgreSQL's id counters) "can have different values on different servers".

The other repair is to forbid anything that can come out different. VoltDB, a database built for speed, copies changes by running the same stored procedures (programs kept inside the database) on every copy. It requires them to give the same result every time. Durable execution met the same rule. A workflow engine rebuilds an order's progress by replaying its code, so that code must make the same choices on every replay. It reads the time and random numbers through the engine, which writes the values into its history. A statement log needs the same rule for SQL, and nothing enforces it.

A statement runs again on every follower. Unless something forces the same result, don't ship statements.

So the log should carry what a statement did, not the statement. PostgreSQL's answer is the most literal one: the exact bytes it changed on disk.

steps: From the labs folder, run the first command below. The leader runs five statements and writes both logs. Follower S runs each statement 350 ms later, with its own clock, and follower R applies the row entries. Then the tail of each log arrives a second time, as it can after a reconnect.

Predict, then run the second command. In it, the leader writes its own now() and random values into each statement before logging it. Which difference goes away, and which one stays?

Statement 4 became two row entries, one for each row it changed. The statement copy made its own reference codes and times, and paid the fee twice when statement 4 arrived again. The row copy is identical to the leader, resend and all. With pin, the statements carry '23c52a1a', 1000010 instead of random() and now(), so codes and times match. sections.h: Sending the disk changes: exact bytes, tied to one version
sections.html:
PostgreSQL went the other way. Like most databases, it already keeps a log for its own sake. Before it changes its data files, it writes a note of the change to its write-ahead log, the WAL. After a crash, it replays the WAL onto the data files, so no committed change is lost (the Storage track's lesson Write-ahead logging and crash recovery builds this). A follower, which PostgreSQL calls a standby, is a server whose recovery never ends. It receives the leader's WAL as it's written, and replays it onto an identical copy of the data files. Oracle's database copies its own disk-level log, the redo log, the same way.

A WAL record doesn't say what the SQL was. It says which bytes changed, and where. PostgreSQL keeps a table's rows in a file split into 8 KB pages, called the heap. Each index, a lookup structure that finds rows by a key, has a file of its own. In this section's Try it, one INSERT of a refund writes four records:

  1. A heap insert: the new row goes into the first page (block 0) of the refunds table's file.
  2. An index insert: the refund's number goes into a page of the table's primary-key index. The primary key is the column that names each row, and a B-tree is the usual kind of index.
  3. A row lock on payment 3, the payment being refunded. A foreign key, the rule that a refund must name a real payment, checks that row and marks it so that nobody deletes it meanwhile.
  4. The commit, which makes the other three count.

In the records, rel 1663/16386/17262 names the storage area, the database and the table's file. There's no now() left to work out and no id to choose: the leader did all of that, and the standby copies the results bit for bit, indexes included. Nothing can drift.

The price is that the log speaks the private language of the storage engine, the part of PostgreSQL that lays data out on disk. Page layouts and index formats may change between major versions, such as 17 and 18. So a PostgreSQL 17 standby can't replay an 18 leader's WAL. That rules out a tempting trick: upgrade the standby first, then make it the leader, and the upgrade costs almost nothing. Instead, all the machines move together, with the pg_upgrade tool and a short outage, or through a copy of rows (next section).

The WAL also describes everything on the server: every database, every index page, every page that cleanup work touched. You can't send one table, and nothing outside PostgreSQL can read it.

So physical replication, as copying the disk-level log is called, is the right format for what lesson 1 asked of a follower: an exact copy, ready to take over. For anything else, it's the wrong one. Next, a log that keeps the exactness and drops the private language.

try.title: Read the WAL records of one INSERT
steps: Start the leader and its standby from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml up -d --wait (about 20 seconds the first time). Docker runs each server in a container, a walled-off space on your computer. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's command-line program, on the leader: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the SQL below. The first INSERT only warms things up; the one you'll read is the second. Copy the two log positions it prints (PostgreSQL calls a position an LSN).

In a shell, decode the WAL between them, using your positions: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -u postgres primary bash -c 'pg_waldump -p $PGDATA/pg_wal -s 0/5003FD8 -e 0/5005D88'. Match each rel number to the file numbers the last query printed.

code.title: psql on the primary
code.html: INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 700, 'customer_request', now()); -- warms up: see the expect SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (3, 750, 'customer_request', now()) RETURNING refund_id; SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS after; SELECT oid AS course FROM pg_database WHERE datname = 'course'; SELECT pg_relation_filenode('refunds') AS refunds, pg_relation_filenode('refunds_pkey') AS refunds_pkey, pg_relation_filenode('payments') AS payments;

try.expect:
The second refund is id 8, between 0/5003FD8 and 0/5005D88 here. Its records (your positions, ids and file numbers will differ):

rmgr: Heap2       len (rec/tot):     53/  7297, tx:          0, lsn: 0/05003FD8, prev 0/05003FB0, desc: PRUNE_ON_ACCESS , isCatalogRel: F, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/1255 blk 47 FPW
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):    111/   111, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005C78, prev 0/05003FD8, desc: INSERT off: 8, flags: 0x00, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/17262 blk 0
rmgr: Btree       len (rec/tot):     64/    64, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005CE8, prev 0/05005C78, desc: INSERT_LEAF off: 8, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/17274 blk 1
rmgr: Heap        len (rec/tot):     54/    54, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005D28, prev 0/05005CE8, desc: LOCK xmax: 852, off: 3, infobits: [LOCK_ONLY, KEYSHR_LOCK], flags: 0x00, blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/17226 blk 0
rmgr: Transaction len (rec/tot):     34/    34, tx:        852, lsn: 0/05005D60, prev 0/05005D28, desc: COMMIT 2026-11-08 06:04:53.554268 UTC

Here course was 16386, refunds 17262, refunds_pkey 17274 and payments 17226. Transaction 852 is the INSERT. The heap record puts the row at item 8 of the table's first page, and the B-tree record adds its key to the index. The lock record is the foreign-key check marking payment 3's row with a key-share lock, which only stops others from deleting the row or changing its key. The commit makes it count. The four add up to 263 bytes, with no SQL and no now() in sight: the commit time is a value the leader already chose. The first line has tx: 0. It's another part of the server cleaning up a page of PostgreSQL's own internal tables, a reminder that the WAL carries everything that happens on the server. Decode from before the first INSERT instead, and you also see FPW records (whole 8 KB pages, logged the first time a page changes after a checkpoint, as the Storage track's lesson explained) and a Sequence record: the id counter logging 32 values ahead.

sections.h: Sending the rows: a log of results
sections.html:
The WAL got one thing right: it carries results, values the leader already worked out, so a follower has nothing to work out again. Its problem is the language of pages and bytes. Say the same results in terms of rows, and you get a logical log, also called row-based. Each entry describes one row. An insert carries every column's new value. An update carries the row's key and its new values, and a delete carries the key. A commit marker closes each transaction, the group of changes that become final together. The leader works out every value once, and the log records results, never the SQL that produced them.

In this section's Try it, the statement UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = amount_minor + 50 WHERE payment_id = 4 adds 50 cents to a refund. PostgreSQL turns it into this row entry:

table public.refunds: UPDATE: refund_id[bigint]:9 payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:350 reason[text]:'duplicate' created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'

The + 50 is gone. The entry says the row now holds 350, and applying it twice still leaves 350. Lesson 1's catch-up can send a follower entries it already has, and a log of results makes that harmless. A change that gives the same result applied twice as applied once is called idempotent. MongoDB, a database that stores records as documents, built its log, the oplog, this way on purpose. Its manual says every oplog entry is idempotent. An update that adds to a balance is recorded with the resulting value, and an update of many documents becomes one entry per document.

A row entry says nothing about pages, so it isn't tied to the storage format. A follower can run a newer major version or a different database, and it can take only some tables. That opens two doors. Upgrades: start a row-log copy on the new version, let it catch up, then move the programs over in minutes. And change data capture: other systems can read the same stream of row changes. Debezium, a program that reads databases' change logs, feeds them this way into Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages. The Stream processing track's lesson Two systems, one truth: dual writes and change data capture builds on it.

MySQL keeps its row log, the binary log, as a second log next to the one its storage engine keeps for crashes. Rows have been its default format since version 5.7. The setting that changes the format, binlog_format, has been marked for removal since 8.0, and the manual expects rows to become the only format. PostgreSQL has no second log. With the setting wal_level = logical, a feature called logical decoding reads the WAL and turns it into row changes through an output plugin, a small add-on that decides the format. pgoutput feeds PostgreSQL's own row-log replication, and test_decoding prints text you can read.

Rows cost more in some places. One UPDATE of 80,000 rows is one statement, but 80,000 row entries. The follower finds each row by its key, so a table with no primary key needs one more setting first (the box below). And PostgreSQL's row log carries no changes to a table's columns and, as of version 18, no values of its id counters (lesson 4 covers what 18 and 19 add).

A log of results can arrive twice and do no harm. Make it the default.

Sometimes, though, the database's own log can't give you the shape you need, and you build one yourself.

try.title: Decode three changes into rows
steps: With the servers from the last Try it running, switch the leader's WAL to the logical level and restart it: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c 'ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_level = logical', then docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml restart primary.

Open psql on the leader (docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course) and run the session below. It creates a replication slot named peek, the leader's note of how far one reader has got, which keeps the changes until someone reads them. Before the last query, predict what the UPDATE's entry will say about amount_minor.

Put the server back: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec primary psql -U sfz -d course -c 'ALTER SYSTEM RESET wal_level' and docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml restart primary. The session dropped the slot first, and that matters: a slot nobody reads keeps WAL on the leader forever (lesson 4).

code.title: psql on the primary
code.html: SHOW wal_level; SELECT slot_name FROM pg_create_logical_replication_slot('peek', 'test_decoding'); INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (4, 300, 'duplicate', now()) RETURNING refund_id; UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = amount_minor + 50 WHERE payment_id = 4; DELETE FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 3 AND amount_minor = 750; -- the last Try it's refund SELECT lsn, xid, data FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes('peek', NULL, NULL); SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('peek');

try.expect:
wal_level is logical. Each transaction comes out between BEGIN and COMMIT, one line per row. (The wide column header is trimmed, and your ids, transaction numbers and positions differ.)

    lsn    | xid |  data
-----------+-----+-------------------------------------------------------------
 0/6000110 | 859 | BEGIN 859
 0/6000178 | 859 | table public.refunds: INSERT: refund_id[bigint]:9 payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:300 reason[text]:'duplicate' created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'
 0/6002228 | 859 | COMMIT 859
 0/6004270 | 860 | BEGIN 860
 0/6004270 | 860 | table public.refunds: UPDATE: refund_id[bigint]:9 payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:350 reason[text]:'duplicate' created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'
 0/6004318 | 860 | COMMIT 860
 0/6004318 | 861 | BEGIN 861
 0/6004318 | 861 | table public.refunds: DELETE: refund_id[bigint]:8
 0/60063B8 | 861 | COMMIT 861
(9 rows)

The INSERT carries every column, including the created_at time that now() produced on the leader. The UPDATE carries the key and the result, 350. The DELETE carries only the key: refund 8, the one from the last Try it. get_changes uses up what it returns, so a second call prints nothing; pg_logical_slot_peek_changes would leave the changes in place.

aside.title: What about a table with no key?
aside.html: A row entry must say which row it changed, and the follower finds that row by its key. PostgreSQL lets you publish a table without a primary key, and its new rows copy fine. Then the first update or delete on the leader fails, inside the program's own transaction, with "cannot update table ... because it does not have a replica identity and publishes updates". Give every published table a primary key first. REPLICA IDENTITY FULL also works, by logging the whole old row with every change, at the price of a bigger log and a slow search on the follower.

sections.h: Building the log yourself with triggers
sections.html:
Sometimes the database's own log won't do. You need one table copied into another kind of database, filtered or reshaped, from an old version that has no logical decoding. Then you capture the changes yourself, with a trigger: a small program the database runs on every change to a table.

The trigger runs on every insert, update and delete, inside the same transaction as the change, and writes a change row into a log table. A separate program reads the log table in order, applies the changes somewhere else, and deletes what it has sent. Slony-I copied PostgreSQL tables to several standbys this way. (Its site now says it hasn't been updated in years, and points to PostgreSQL's built-in logical replication.) Bucardo used triggers to copy between databases in both directions.

It's a logical log written by hand. It carries row values: the Try it stores each row as JSON, a common text format, with to_jsonb(NEW). So it keeps the logical log's strengths, and you pick the tables, the shape and the destination. It costs more, and the cost lands inside every change the program makes, because each write becomes two, plus the trigger's own work. In the Try it, 20,000 inserts took 76 ms without the trigger and 191 ms with it.

Triggers also miss what nobody wrote them for. A new table has no trigger yet. TRUNCATE, a command that empties a whole table at once, doesn't fire triggers that run once per row. And a change to a table's columns isn't a row change at all.

The idea lives on in two places. Audit tables, which record every change for people to check later, keep the log table as the product. And in a pattern called the transactional outbox, the program writes an event row in the same transaction as its data, and a separate program sends it on to Kafka. The Stream processing track picks that up.

Here are the four logs side by side:

Statement Disk changes (WAL) Rows (logical) Trigger
An entry says the SQL text bytes at a page and offset a row's key and values a row's values, in your format
The follower ends up identical only if every statement gives the same result everywhere yes, bit for bit yes if the trigger is right
Versions must match no yes no no
Other systems can read it no no yes yes
An UPDATE of 80,000 rows 1 entry 80,000+ page records 80,000 entries 80,000 log rows, inside the transaction

Every column of that table shares one limit. However exact the log, a follower applies it later than the leader wrote it. Next, we'll find out what that delay does to someone reading from a follower.

try.title: Capture changes with a trigger, and time what it costs
steps: With the servers running, save the script below as capture.sql in the labs folder, and pipe it into psql on the leader: docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml exec -T primary psql -U sfz -d course < capture.sql.
Before you run it: in the timed part, the first 20,000 inserts fire the trigger and the second 20,000 don't. How much slower do you expect the first batch to be?
When you're done with this lesson's Try-its, docker compose -f env/postgres-ha.yml down -v removes both servers and their data.

code.title: capture.sql
code.html: CREATE TABLE refunds_changes ( change_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, op text NOT NULL, refund_id bigint NOT NULL, row_data jsonb, changed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT clock_timestamp() ); CREATE FUNCTION log_refund_change() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN IF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN INSERT INTO refunds_changes (op, refund_id) VALUES (TG_OP, OLD.refund_id); RETURN OLD; END IF; INSERT INTO refunds_changes (op, refund_id, row_data) VALUES (TG_OP, NEW.refund_id, to_jsonb(NEW)); RETURN NEW; END $$; CREATE TRIGGER refunds_capture AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON refunds FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_refund_change(); INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (5, 420, 'fraud', now()) RETURNING refund_id \gset UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = 400 WHERE refund_id = :refund_id; DELETE FROM refunds WHERE refund_id = :refund_id; SELECT change_id, op, refund_id, row_data FROM refunds_changes ORDER BY change_id; \timing on INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 6, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 20000); ALTER TABLE refunds DISABLE TRIGGER refunds_capture; INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) SELECT 6, 100, 'customer_request', now() FROM generate_series(1, 20000); \timing off DROP TRIGGER refunds_capture ON refunds; DROP FUNCTION log_refund_change(); DROP TABLE refunds_changes; DELETE FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 6;

try.expect:
The log table holds the three changes, each with the row as JSON (your ids and times differ):

 change_id |   op   | refund_id |                                                           row_data
-----------+--------+-----------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
         1 | INSERT |        10 | {"reason": "fraud", "refund_id": 10, "created_at": "2026-11-08T06:05:29.475533+00:00", "payment_id": 5, "amount_minor": 420}
         2 | UPDATE |        10 | {"reason": "fraud", "refund_id": 10, "created_at": "2026-11-08T06:05:29.475533+00:00", "payment_id": 5, "amount_minor": 400}
         3 | DELETE |        10 |
(3 rows)

Timing is on.
INSERT 0 20000
Time: 190.586 ms
ALTER TABLE
Time: 0.433 ms

Time: 75.503 ms
Timing is off.

With the trigger, the batch took about 2.5 times as long. Running the two batches in the other order gave the same ratio (73 ms without, 187 ms with), so it isn't a warm-up effect. Your times depend on your computer. The ratio is the point, and every extra millisecond was spent inside the inserting transaction.

opening:
Picture a café with two branches that keep the same price list. When the owner changes prices at the first branch, she texts the manager of the second: "Raise every price by 10 cents, and write today's date at the top." He reads the text the next morning, so his list carries a different date. Then her phone says "not delivered" and sends the text again, and the second branch raises its prices twice.

Sending the instruction feels like the natural choice. It's short, and anyone can read it. But the second branch does the work again, at another time, and gets another answer.

In One leader, many followers, the leader wrote every change into a numbered log, and the followers applied it in order. We never said what one entry of that log says. In this lesson, we'll write the same changes three ways: as the instruction, as the exact bytes changed on disk, and as the new rows. Then we'll watch which followers drift. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a price list sent as an instruction, which the second branch worked out again, and got wrong twice. A log of statements does the same. A log of disk bytes copies exactly, but only to the same version, and a log of rows copies the results anywhere.

On the course's PostgreSQL leader, or any PostgreSQL you can reach, run SHOW wal_level;. replica, the default, means it can feed standbys that copy its disk changes. logical means it can also give out a log of rows.

Next, we'll look at followers that copy the log perfectly but late, and ask what someone reading from them sees.

compare.title: One UPDATE, two logs

a.label: Statement-based
a.title: what the follower receives
a.html: UPDATE refunds SET amount_minor = amount_minor + 50 WHERE payment_id = 4; -- one entry, whatever the number of rows -- the follower evaluates it against its own data -- sent twice: amount_minor goes up by 100

b.label: Row-based (PostgreSQL logical decoding)
b.title: what test_decoding printed (one line, wrapped)
b.html:
BEGIN 860
table public.refunds: UPDATE: refund_id[bigint]:9
  payment_id[bigint]:4 amount_minor[bigint]:350
  reason[text]:'duplicate'
  created_at[timestamp with time zone]:'2026-11-08 06:05:14.59426+00'
COMMIT 860

-- one entry per changed row, with the results
-- sent twice: amount_minor is still 350

compare.note: The statement is shorter and describes the intent, so the follower has to work it out again, and its answer depends on the follower's data, its clock and luck. The row entry is longer and describes only the outcome, so any follower that applies it ends up with the same row, however many times it arrives. Most databases log rows, and keep statements, if at all, for cases where the leader can prove a statement gives the same result everywhere.

worked.title: Read a PostgreSQL change stream from Kotlin, safely

steps.say: Create a logical replication slot once. The slot remembers how far its reader has confirmed, and the leader keeps the WAL from that point on, until the reader moves the slot forward.
steps.code: -- needs wal_level = logical SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('refunds_cdc', 'test_decoding');

steps.say: Poll with peek, which reads changes without using them up, so a crash between reading and applying loses nothing. Logical decoding gives out only committed transactions, in the order they committed.
steps.code: data class Change(val lsn: String, val xid: String, val data: String) fun peek(conn: java.sql.Connection, max: Int = 1_000): List<Change> = conn.prepareStatement( "SELECT lsn::text, xid::text, data FROM pg_logical_slot_peek_changes('refunds_cdc', NULL, ?)" ).use { ps -> ps.setInt(1, max) ps.executeQuery().use { rs -> buildList { while (rs.next()) add(Change(rs.getString(1), rs.getString(2), rs.getString(3))) } } }

steps.say: Apply each change by its key, so a change seen twice does no harm. Use an upsert (insert the row, or update it if the key is already there) for inserts and updates, and a delete for deletes. Parsing test_decoding's text is fine for a demo. Real code uses pgoutput over a replication connection, or Debezium.
steps.code: -- in the target database, for each INSERT or UPDATE line INSERT INTO refunds_copy (refund_id, payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (:refund_id, :payment_id, :amount_minor, :reason, :created_at) ON CONFLICT (refund_id) DO UPDATE SET payment_id = EXCLUDED.payment_id, amount_minor = EXCLUDED.amount_minor, reason = EXCLUDED.reason, created_at = EXCLUDED.created_at; -- for each DELETE line DELETE FROM refunds_copy WHERE refund_id = :refund_id;

steps.say: Only after the copy has committed, tell the slot how far you got. The leader may then recycle the WAL before that point. If you crash before this step, the next peek returns the same changes, and the upserts absorb them.
steps.code: SELECT pg_replication_slot_advance('refunds_cdc', :last_applied_lsn::pg_lsn);

steps.say: When the reader is retired, drop the slot. A slot that nobody moves forward keeps every WAL file after its position, until the leader's disk is full (lesson 4).

lab.title: Replaying statements against replaying rows
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder; they need no Docker. All 21 fail, because the leader builds its row log with exercise 1. Read ReplicationLog.kt: Server.execute runs statements with the server's own clock, random numbers, id counter and row order, and Leader.run writes both logs.

Exercise 1, rowEvents(before, after): one event per changed row, in id order. Run RowEventsTest, then StatementReplayTest. It now passes, and each of its tests is one way a statement copy drifts: its own now(), its own random(), a fee charged twice, a LIMIT that picks other rows, and swapped ids.

Exercise 2, Server.applyRow: apply an event so that applying it twice changes nothing. Also move nextId past every copied id, so that a promoted follower doesn't hand out an id it already holds (lesson 1's GitHub bug). RowReplayTest replays every drift case with rows.

Exercise 3, pin: replace now() and random() with the leader's values before logging, as MySQL does for NOW(). PinTest shows what that fixes and what it can't. Then ReplayPropertyTest runs 100 random workloads for each property.
hints: rowEvents: walk (before.keys + after.keys).sorted() and compare before[id] with after[id]. Only in after is an insert, only in before is a delete, and in both but different is an update.
applyRow: a when (event) that puts event.row for inserts and updates and removes the id for deletes; then if (event !is RowEvent.Deleted) nextId = maxOf(nextId, event.id + 1).
pin: only Statement.Insert has values to pin. Use statement.copy(ref = ..., createdAt = ...), and call on.randomRef() and on.now() only for the parts that are Ref.Random and Ts.Now.
A property test that fails prints the seed, the workload size and the lag. Paste them into a plain test, and print leader.rows and follower.rows side by side.

drill.title: Turn a change into row events
drill.prompt: From memory, write rowEvents(before, after). It gets the table before and after one statement, as maps from id to row, and returns an Inserted, Updated or Deleted event for every changed row, in id order. Then say in one sentence why a follower that applies these events twice ends up with the same table.

answer.html: fun rowEvents(before: Map<Long, Row>, after: Map<Long, Row>): List<RowEvent> = (before.keys + after.keys).sorted().mapNotNull { id -> val old = before[id] val new = after[id] when { old == null && new != null -> RowEvent.Inserted(new) old != null && new == null -> RowEvent.Deleted(id) old != null && new != null && old != new -> RowEvent.Updated(new) else -> null } } // Twice is harmless: each event says what the row IS (or that it is gone), never what to add to it.

recap: A replication log can carry the statements, the disk-level changes (PostgreSQL's WAL) or the changed rows. Each is a different answer to "what does a follower need to repeat this change?"

Statement logs are short and readable, and they drift: now(), random(), new ids handed out in another order, LIMIT without ORDER BY, "add to it" changes sent twice and triggers all come out differently on a follower. MySQL records its clock for NOW() and flags the rest as unsafe.
Copying the WAL gives an exact copy, indexes included, but ties every machine to the same major version and to the whole server. It's the right format for a copy you fail over to.

A logical log carries each row's key and resulting values, so applying it twice does no harm, and followers can run other versions or other databases. MySQL's binary log, PostgreSQL's logical decoding and MongoDB's oplog work this way.
Triggers build a logical log by hand: flexible, but they double the work inside every change, and they miss what nobody wrote them for.
The limit: every log, however exact, reaches the followers later than the leader wrote it.

explain.prompt: A friend asks why PostgreSQL has two kinds of replication, physical and logical, when "replication means copying the changes". Explain what each one copies, and when you'd use it.
explain.answer: Both copy the changes, but they describe them in different languages. Physical replication sends PostgreSQL's write-ahead log, which says which bytes on which page of which file changed. A standby replays that onto an identical copy of the files, so it ends up exact, indexes and all, and ready to take over if the leader dies. The catch is that this log is in PostgreSQL's private disk format. The standby must run the same major version, it gets every database on the server, and nothing else can read it. Logical replication turns the same log into row changes: this row was added with these values, this key now has these values, this key was deleted. Rows don't depend on the disk format, so the receiver can run a newer version, take only some tables, or not be PostgreSQL at all. That's what you use to upgrade with little downtime, and to feed other systems like Kafka. It costs more for big changes, one entry per row, it needs a key on every table, and it doesn't carry changes to a table's columns. So: physical for the copy you fail over to, and logical for moving data somewhere different.

deeper.html:
MySQL's row entries have a setting for how much of the row they carry. binlog_row_image is FULL by default (every column, before and after the change), and MINIMAL logs only the key and the changed columns. That makes the binary log smaller, but readers such as Debezium see less of each row.

PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adds logical replication of sequence values, the id counters, which closes one of the gaps this lesson listed. Check the final release notes before you rely on it. Changes to a table's columns still aren't copied logically: tools apply them on both sides themselves.

State machine replication is the general idea behind making statements safe. If every copy starts in the same state and applies the same commands, each giving the same result every time, in the same order, the copies stay identical. VoltDB uses it for whole stored procedures. Raft and Paxos (the Consistency and consensus track) agree on the order of the commands, and giving the same result every time is the program's side of the bargain. A workflow engine's replay, from Durable execution, is the same contract for one workflow.

MongoDB's oplog lives in a special collection of fixed size, local.oplog.rs. Since MongoDB 5.0, you can't write to it by hand on a replica set. Its size, 5% of free disk by default and kept between 990 MB and 50 GB, sets how far back it reaches: how long a follower can be away and still catch up from its position, as in lesson 1.

Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6 describes the same three log formats, and points out that a logical log is also the natural input for change data capture, which this course picks up in the Stream processing track.
